title: Chapter 37 – Pebble
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

He tells no one. That is the first mistake, and he knows it is a mistake as he makes it.

The needle that pointed into the forest is back in its sheath of black cloth under his bed, and the thing it pointed at has not moved in two nights. Jian can feel it faintly at the edge of his sense whenever he lies awake: a small cold shape, curled tight, not quite alive and not quite dying. It does not call. It does not struggle. It simply holds on.

On the third night he stops arguing with himself.

Whatever it is, it is hurt, and it is close to the wall. If a hunter finds it before I do, I will never know what it was. He dresses in the dark, in a gray tunic and dark leggings, with the knife in his belt and the Seven Seam Needles in a wrapped roll against his spine. He checks the pouch under his tunic. In it are the nine pins of the Nine-Pin Belt and Hu's four practice pins, a coil of silk cord, a bag of ground capsaicin, a dozen paper Fire Seals from the dead man's slip, and the last Royal Spirit Chain Father drew for him.

One chain. It is not enough. He considers the weight of what he is carrying, and the weight of what he is not. It will have to be.

He leaves by the eastern postern, at the hour of the hare, and does not wake the guard.

* * *

The outer forest in late autumn is a cold, wet, ticking place.

Leaves lie in drifts under the beeches, black and slick. The giant cedars stand in their shrouds of fog, and between them the dawn comes up thin and silver. He walks with the Still Water Veil folded close, and the Veil Step carried through every stride, and he counts the cost in breaths. Eleven minutes of this and he will be running on his reserve. So he walks a hundred paces, and rests, and walks again.

The thing he is following does not move. But as he draws nearer, the tug in his sense grows sharper, and a second thing makes itself known. It is not small and it is not frightened. It is cold, and wet, and it smells of iron and salt.

Blood.

He stops. He lowers himself behind the root of a fallen cedar and lets his reach spread outward, slowly, a hand over a pond.

They are two hundred paces east of the thing he is hunting. Two men, moving together, about thirty paces apart. They are not hurrying. They walk with the loose, easy gait of men who have done this before and know they are not being watched, and each carries something. He cannot tell what. He only feels the shape of their Qi, and it is the thin, red, sticky shape that he has met twice in his life and has not forgotten.

Blood Shadow. Two of them. Drip stage. He measures. One is steady and heavy, a Qi Refining eighth-stage, with a wide dull core like an old stone. The other is lighter and quicker, sixth or seventh, with a sharp edge to his Qi, a sound like a wire being drawn.

They are hunting it, too.

He does not know why that frightens him so much. He does not know why, an instant later, he finds that he has already decided.

* * *

He finds it by midday.

It lies in the root-cleft of a huge, dead oak at the bottom of a damp gully, a place where three stone ribs of the mountain come together and the ground sinks into a bowl. The oak has been dead for a century. Its trunk is hollow, a black tunnel fifteen feet across, and between two of its buttress roots there is a crack in the bark just wide enough for a dog to crawl through.

He kneels at the mouth of it with the Veil folded close and looks in.

For a moment he sees only dark.

Then the dark moves, and two eyes open in it, black, enormous, wet. They are the eyes of a creature that has never been afraid of anything and has discovered, very recently, that it ought to be.

Pangolin.

He knows it from the old bestiaries in the library. A scaled thing, a burrower. This one is a hatchling, perhaps a month out of the egg, no larger than a loaf of bread. Its scales are pale gray-brown and smooth, overlapping like the pebbles of a river bank, with a faint translucent sheen on each that catches the light in a hundred small places. It has curled itself into a tight armored ball, with its nose tucked under its tail. Along its flank, between the third and fourth row of scales, a long gash runs, black and raw, and the edges of the cut are crusted with something dark and crawling.

It is a blood-chain wound. He has seen one before, on Hu's arm. The cut is not deep. But the chain that made it was soaked in something, and the poison is working through the muscle.

He does not scan it.

He has been taught that a scan is a thing you do to a stranger, from a distance, when you do not wish to be known. He is not sure why he knows it is wrong to do it now. He only knows that the creature in the oak has already felt his sense, and has gone stiff and silent, waiting for a blow.

He puts his hand out slowly, palm up, and lets the Veil fall.

It is a risk. If the creature were large it would be a foolish one. But it is not large, and it is not a predator, and in the instant that the Veil drops he feels something touch him, lightly, tentatively, as a tongue touches a stranger's hand. A thread of awareness, thin as a hair, reaching out from the dark of the oak.

It tastes him.

It is tasting my Qi, he thinks. It is tasting the shape of it. The fold.

And then, so suddenly that he almost cries out, a wave of feeling goes through him, not a sound but a sensation, wordless and enormous. It is a hunger like a cold stone in the stomach. It is a fear that has been alone too long. And under both, very quiet, a small, bright, startled recognition, as if the creature had been walking in a world of straight lines for a month and had just seen a curve.

Seam, it says, without words. Seam. You are folded. You are a seam.

Jian stares into the dark with his hand outstretched and his heart pounding.

He takes a small pouch from his belt, the one with the crystals of salt he scraped from the sluice pan at the granary, gray and coarse, faintly bright with a trace of spirit iron. He tips a few grains onto his palm. He holds it out.

For a long time, nothing happens.

Then the pale scales loosen. A long, narrow snout appears from under the tail. A tongue the color of a petal flicks out and touches the salt. And the creature gives a small, shaky, pitiful sigh and begins to eat out of his hand, with its eyes closed, as if it had not tasted anything in a week.

* * *

"Do not make a sound," Jian whispers, "and do not bite."

It does not bite. It lies in the crook of his arm, light as a loaf, warm as a stone left in the sun, and looks up at him with those enormous wet eyes. A wave of something goes through him again. Not hunger this time, but a trembling, dazed, absurd gratitude. It is not a language. It does not have words. But he understands it as clearly as if it had spoken.

Salt. Good. You are not the hurt one. You are the warm one.

He cleans the wound with a pad of cloth and a splash of boiled water from his flask. He lays a Wound Knit paste on it, from the little jar he took out of the dead man's pouch, and binds it with a strip of linen. The creature winces and does not move. It trusts him with its whole body, with the casual, appalling confidence of something that has never been lied to.

It is going to be a problem, he thinks.

Then he feels the other two.

They are very near now. A hundred paces, at the top of the gully, and closing. He had been so absorbed in the creature that he had let his sense go slack, and now he feels them like a cold finger laid on the back of his neck. They are not hurrying. One is walking. The other has stopped, and is bending down, and is touching something on the ground with the tips of his fingers.

A blood trail, Jian thinks. The creature's. It must have dragged itself through the gully the first night, and bled on every stone.

He has perhaps three minutes.

* * *

It is not a plan. It is a list again. He builds it in his head as he moves, with the creature wrapped in his tunic and the pins already out of the pouch, and each item falls into place with a little click like a bolt in a lock.

The gully is a bowl. It has one way in, a narrow trail of leaf-mold along the east side, and one way out, a steep scramble up a slope of loose stone to the west. The oak lies in the middle. Whoever comes in must follow the blood trail to the oak. The blood trail runs along the trail.

I cannot beat them. Not two of them, not Drip stage, not at once. He makes himself say it. I can beat what they walk into.

He runs the length of the trail in the first minute, setting pins. He does not trust the belt's modes. He sets them by hand, one by one, pressed into the black mold under the leaves, six in a hexagon at the mouth of the gully where the trail narrows between two boulders. He pours a thin line of capsaicin powder along the trail beyond the hexagon, and covers it with leaves. He tears three Fire Seals in half and hangs them from the low branches on thread. And at the foot of the oak, where the blood trail ends, he lays down the four pins of the binding in a square, and sets the creature in the middle.

It looks at him with enormous eyes. It does not move.

"Stay," he whispers. "Please."

It makes a small dry sound in its throat, like a pebble turning over. It tucks its nose under its tail.

He climbs the dead oak. It is not hard. The bark is soft with rot, and the first buttress gives him a foothold, and from there it is only a scramble to the broad branch thirty feet up, where the crown of the tree once spread, now bare and silver. He lies along it on his belly with the Veil wrapped tight and the Veil Step ready, and the Seven Seam Needles laid out along the bark in a row. The Chain is in his left hand. The knife is in his right.

He waits. His heart is beating very hard.

Steady. They will come in single file. The heavy one first, because he is the tracker. The light one behind, to cover the rear.

He is right.

* * *

They enter the gully together, the heavy one first.

He is a broad, flat-faced man in a brown leather harness, with a bald head and a thick neck and a bowl of black bone hanging from his belt, wide as a washbasin and carved with spirals. It is the same kind of bowl Jian saw in a cave a year ago, and the memory goes through him like cold water. The man's eyes are half-lidded, almost sleepy. He walks with his head down, following the dark smears on the stones.

Behind him comes the lighter one, thin and quick, a man in a rust-colored cloak with a hooked chain looped around his right forearm. The chain's links are black and glistening. Its end is a barbed hook the length of a finger. He moves like a heron, lifting each foot clear and setting it down with exaggerated care, and his eyes never stop moving.

They reach the boulders.

"It bled a lot," the heavy one says in a bored voice. "It will be near. Smell that? Salt."

"It will be dead by now."

"Then the Elder will be displeased. He said alive."

"The Elder says many things." The thin man laughs. "A seamwalker, he said. Little more than a lizard. I do not see why—"

The heavy one's boot comes down on the third leaf from the left boulder.

Six.

The hexagon fires.

Pale silver light runs between the pins in a ring around the two men's feet. The heavy one stiffens with his foot in mid-step. The light one, a pace behind, has just lifted his heel, and the edge of the ring catches him across the ankle, and he goes down hard on one knee with a curse that is cut off in the middle.

It is not a clean snare. The light one was half outside it, and he is already tearing his leg free, with a wet ripping sound. The heavy one is fully caught. He stands rigid, with a startled blank face, and his bone bowl swinging at his hip.

Six breaths against a Qi Refining eighth-stage, Jian thinks. Four against the quick one if he is half out.

He does not hesitate. He throws the chain.

It is the last Royal Spirit Chain. It leaves his hand in a streak of gold and opens in the air like a flower, and it goes for the heavy man first, a coil around his chest, a loop around his throat, because the heavy one is the dangerous one, the one who can move when the binding ends. The gold bites. The man's face goes dark red. He tries to lift his arms and cannot.

The light one has torn free. He is up. He is backing away along the trail with the hook in his hand, and his eyes find the oak, the top of it, the thin dark line against the sky, and Jian sees understanding go across his face like a shadow.

"Above!" he shrieks. "In the tree—"

The hook flies.

It is not a throw. It is a flick of the wrist, and the chain behind it uncoils in a long black rattle, and the barbed point comes up the trunk of the oak like a snake. Jian rolls. The hook thuds into the bark a hand's width from his ribs. It tears loose a long strip of rotten wood, and the chain whips back, and he feels his sleeve part and a line of cold run down his upper arm.

He is slashed. The bleeding is warm and then very hot. He grits his teeth and does not cry out.

Do not run. Do not fight him. Find the seam.

What seam?

And then it comes to him, a flash of something that is not his own thought. It is the creature at the foot of the oak. It is a feeling, a tug, a thin, bright, urgent signal, passing through the thread between them. It is not fear. It is not hunger. It is attention. A small mind has fixed itself on the thin man, and is turning, very slowly, as a compass needle turns, and showing him something.

There.

It is a place. A tiny place, at the man's right collarbone. Jian looks at it and sees nothing. Then the creature's feeling presses against his own, and the world shifts, and he sees.

A barrier. A thin, dull, rust-colored shell of Qi around the man's torso, thin as the skin on milk. Not a talisman. A natural defense, a trained shield that every Qi Refining cultivator who has reached the sixth stage can raise without thinking. It is flawless. It is smooth. And at the right collarbone, where the strap of the chain crosses the cloak, a hair's breadth of the shell is missing.

A seam.

It is not a mistake. It is not a weakness. It is where two parts of a thing meet. The shell is raised in two halves, front and back, and joined at the shoulders, and the joining is never perfect. A trained fighter learns to cover it with his arm. This man has the chain across it, and the chain has moved.

Left needle, Jian thinks. Thread one. Go.

The first needle leaves the bark. It crosses thirty paces of cold air faster than he can think, a gray-blue line drawn from his mind to the man's shoulder, and it finds the gap and does not stop. The barrier does not break. It parts, gently, like a curtain, and the needle slides through into the muscle above the collarbone, and passes between two ribs, and Jian pushes the thread of Qi along its length and twists.

The thin man opens his mouth. No sound comes out. His eyes go wide and then fixed. He takes one step, and another, and his hand reaches for the hook, and then the chain falls out of his fingers and he folds quietly onto the leaves.

Jian drops from the oak.

It is a long fall and a hard one. He lands on his knees on the bank, with a spike of pain in his left thigh, and he is already running for the heavy man, who stands bound and bellowing in the golden coil. The chain is cracking. Gold dust is already sifting from it in a glittering rain. The man's thick arms are shaking with effort and the chain is bending.

Two breaths.

The bowl. He sees it with perfect clarity. The black bone bowl hanging at the man's hip, with its carved spirals, and the cold gleam of the blood-oil inside. A thing meant to burn.

He does not go for the man. He goes for the bowl.

His knife takes the cord at the man's belt and the bowl swings free, and he catches it in both hands and spins it, and the oil flies out of it in a long dark arc. It is cold. It smells of iron. It spatters across the man's chest and face, and across the golden chain, and the man screams, a high raw sound.

"Fire," Jian says, and throws the torn Fire Seal.

The oil catches.

It does not burn orange. It burns white and cold, with a chill like a mouthful of ice, and where it touches the man's skin the skin goes gray and slack. He staggers back, clawing at his face, and the chain gives with a great snap, and he comes forward in a stumbling lunge with his huge hand outstretched.

Needle two.

It finds the seam at the base of the skull. There is no gap there. But the white fire has eaten into the barrier, thinning it, burning a hole the size of a coin, and the needle is through before the hand can close on Jian's throat. The man stops in mid-stride. He sways. He goes down on his face in the leaves with his fingers a hand's breadth from Jian's boots.

It is very quiet in the gully.

* * *

Jian sits down on the bank. He does not mean to. His legs simply decline to hold him.

The thin man lies on his back where he fell. The heavy one lies on his face. The white fire has guttered out. The cold stink of blood-oil hangs in the air, and the dead leaves around the oak are blackened in a ring.

His arm hurts. He looks at it. The slash runs from shoulder to elbow, long and shallow, and the blood has soaked through his sleeve. He binds it with the last of the linen and a strip torn from his cloak, with clumsy shaking fingers, and thinks, very clearly: I should be shaking more than this.

Something touches his knee.

It is the creature. It has crept out of the square of pins, which have faded to dull gray, and has come across the leaf-mold to sit against his leg. It looks up at him with its enormous eyes. It is trembling from nose to tail, and it presses its flank against him and makes the small dry pebble-turning sound.

A flood of feeling comes through him. It is hunger, and fear, and a wild, shaky joy, and under all of it, something very warm.

You are alive. You are alive. You are alive.

"Yes," Jian says, and his voice breaks. "I am. So are you."

And then something happens that he does not understand.

It starts in the center of his chest, where the fragment lies. A warmth. A faint, low hum. It spreads outward through his ribs, and down his arms, and along the thread of awareness that runs from his mind to the creature's. For an instant he feels the two of them as one thing, a single shape in the wet cold gully, with a line of light drawn between. He feels the creature's heartbeat. He feels the small stubborn hunger of it, the faint pulse of its Qi, the way the world looks to something that sees every gap and every join.

Then it is gone, and he is only sitting on a bank with a wounded boy's arm and a lizard against his knee.

He reads it, and then he reads it again, and then he does something he has never done in this world: he laughs aloud, a short helpless sound that startles a bird out of the oak.

"Pebble," he says. It comes out of him before he has thought. He looks at the pale scales, the smooth round shape, the river-stone gleam of the little head. "You look like a pebble. That is what I am going to call you."

The creature tilts its head. A feeling comes down the thread, uncertain, then warm. Pebble. Pebble. Salt.

"Yes," Jian says. "And salt."

* * *

The bodies are a problem, and he solves it badly.

He cannot bury them. He does not have time, and the ground is hard. He cannot carry them. He cannot leave them where a patrol might find them, with the Blood Shadow's marks on their harness and a pair of Seam Needle wounds that no forest beast could make. So he does what Hu would have told him not to, and what Hu would not have forgiven him for not doing.

He takes the bowl, the black bone bowl with its spirals, from where it fell in the leaves. There is a little blood-oil left in the bottom, a finger's depth, cold and clear. He sets it between the two bodies and touches a Fire Seal to it.

The white fire rises, soft and silent. It does not light the gully. It takes the cloaks, the leather, the skin, the bone, as ice takes warm glass, and in the span of a hundred breaths there is nothing left but two small drifts of gray ash and a stain on the stones. The bowl itself, the last of it, melts and runs and is gone.

He sprinkles a handful of leaves on the ash and walks away with the pins in his pouch and a creature in his tunic.

They will know, he thinks. Not how. Not who. But the Blood Shadow will know that two of its people did not come home. He does not like the shape of that thought. He turns it over, from the east, from the north, from the high cold side where the Elder stands in the dark, and it does not get any smaller.

The Elder. The heavy one said it twice. Somewhere in the Pool stage a man has been given a name for what Jian has just picked up out of the leaves, and he wants it alive. A day ago the Blood Shadow was only a shape in Hu's face. Now it is looking at him.

Whatever he sends next will be better.

He sets his shoulder against the wind, and begins the long climb home.

* * *

That night, in the dark of the small room he shares with nobody, the creature sleeps on his pillow in a nest of rolled blankets with its nose under its tail. It breathes slowly. Its flank rises and falls. The wound has closed to a thin pink line, and a faint warmth has crept back into the gray-brown scales.

Jian lies awake, with a cloth on his arm and a mind that will not stop.

It will have to be fed. He thinks of salt. It will have to be hidden. He thinks of Mother, of Hu, of Lin Yue, who is six and cannot keep a secret from a stick. It will have to be trained, and I do not know what it is.

A seamwalker. He does not know the word. There is nothing in the library about it, and he has been through every shelf. They said a seamwalker. They said the Elder wanted it alive.

Something touches the edge of his mind, light as a falling leaf.

It is not a word. It is not a sound. It is a picture, drifting up the thread between them out of the depth of a sleeping creature's dream. He sees it at the edge of his vision, soft and gray and shimmering, like a thing seen through water.

A tree. A single tree, with wide, pale leaves that give off a faint silver light, growing in a place with no sky. Under it a surface of still black water. Around it, row upon row of other trees, a whole orchard of them, standing in a silence so old that it has no edges.

He lies very still.

Where is that?

The picture trembles, and fades, and the thread goes quiet. The creature on the pillow lets out a small, contented sigh, and settles deeper into the blankets.

And in the dark, in the small cold room, a youth of eighteen with a bandaged arm lies and stares at the ceiling, and does not sleep for a long time.
